pulls.title: Add "Agents on the Shared Message Bus" section on A2A
pulls.author: OR13
pulls.body:
## Summary

Elaborates on the utility of the **Shared Message Bus**, framing it as the first venue where agent-to-agent (A2A) collaboration surfaces in most organizations.

New top-level section **"Agents on the Shared Message Bus"** (placed after *Evolving Roles in Agentic Product Delivery*, before *Managing Your Agent*), making four points:

1. Organizations already run channels where people collaborate (IRC, Slack, Teams); Agents first arrive onto those existing channels.
2. Agents appear in two forms — as standalone identities, and acting on behalf of / impersonating the humans they serve (cross-references the Impersonation security section).
3. As Agents pursue business objectives they address one another: A2A is *already happening*, mediated by existing human communications platforms rather than a new agent-only protocol.
4. The benefit is legibility — non-technical stakeholders can follow, contribute to, and review these discussions without special tooling.

Also adds an explicit `{#impersonation}` anchor to the Impersonation heading so the new section can cross-reference it.

## Points for review

- **Placement** — I put this as a standalone top-level section between *Evolving Roles* and *Managing Your Agent*. Alternatives: fold into *Managing Your People* (which already discusses the bus + Proxy Dictation), or place earlier as foundational context. Easy to move.
- **"A2A" as prose vs. defined term** — introduced inline as "agent-to-agent (A2A)" rather than as a capitalized Terminology entry. If A2A should become a formal defined Term, say so.
- **A2A-protocol framing** — the closing contrasts reusing human channels with a hypothetical "agent-only protocol." Kept descriptive (a trade-off, not a verdict) to avoid appearing to disparage emerging A2A protocol work. Flag if you want it more/less pointed.

## Build

Rebuilds clean via `kramdown-rfc` + `xml2rfc` (the `make` venv is currently broken locally — see note below); `{{impersonation}}` resolves to the real section anchor. Only the pre-existing `[1m]` link-ID warning remains, unrelated to this change.

> Note: `make` fails locally because `lib/.venv` points at a broken Python. The build was verified by invoking `kramdown-rfc` / `xml2rfc` directly. Happy to open a separate PR to repair the venv if useful.

pulls.title: Add self-identifying marker (shibboleth) subsection on impersonation
pulls.author: OR13
pulls.body:
## Summary

Adds a concrete, prompt-based mitigation for the impersonation risk on shared channels: a new subsection **"A Shibboleth for Agent-Generated Content"** under *Agents on the Shared Message Bus*.

The mitigation: instruct the Agent, in its persistent Context, to prefix **every** message with a fixed, conspicuous marker, so any reader can tell at a glance the content was generated by an Agent rather than written by the human whose channel it shares. Illustrated with a real team member's rule:

> `omg bestie <short, appropriate opener> 💅`

The subsection then relates the pattern to a **Shibboleth** (new informative reference to the Wikipedia article), noting it *inverts* the classical use — historically a shibboleth proved in-group membership; here it is a tell the Agent emits to mark itself as machine-generated. It closes with the limits, which reinforce the existing **Impersonation** security section: a convention-only marker is a cooperative signal, not an authenticated one — an Agent may drop it (error, Context Rot) and an adversary can trivially forge it — so it `MUST NOT` be relied on as proof of authorship; the platform controls in `{{impersonation}}` remain necessary under adversarial conditions.

## Editorial choices for review

- **Placement** — added as a `##` subsection of the *Agents on the Shared Message Bus* section (merged in #1), rather than in the *Impersonation* security section, to keep the Security Considerations' normative language uncluttered while giving the concrete example room. Cross-linked both ways. Easy to relocate into Security Considerations if you'd prefer.
- **Genericized the colleague's name** — your example named "Justin"; I replaced it with "the human I work for" to avoid putting a real individual's name in a published I-D. Kept the authentic first-person voice and the literal `💅` marker otherwise verbatim. Say the word if you'd rather name them (or use a placeholder like `<manager>`).
- **Literal emoji** — the draft is `v: 3`, so the 💅 builds clean in both HTML and text output (verified, no new warnings). If a future ASCII-only rendering is a concern we can switch to a described form.

## Build

Rebuilds clean via `kramdown-rfc` + `xml2rfc` (HTML and text); `{{SHIBBOLETH}}` and both `{{impersonation}}` cross-references resolve. Only the pre-existing `[1m]` link-ID warning remains, unrelated to this change. (`make` itself is still blocked by the broken `lib/.venv`.)

pulls.title: Verifiable delegation and attribution guidance; add Michael Lavelle as co-author
pulls.author: MJL40635
pulls.body:
## Summary

Folds the accountable-delegation pattern from our verifiable agent coordination work into the draft, in its informational register, and proposes adding Michael Lavelle (Tradeverifyd) as a co-author.

The Security Considerations already call for least-privilege delegation and for an auditable binding between an action, the identity that authorized it, and the Agent that performed it. This PR names the emerging technique that makes those properties verifiable rather than only recorded, and points at the ratified building blocks it composes.

## Changes

- New Security Considerations subsection "Verifiable Delegation and Attributable Action": decentralized identifiers for identity, object-capability tokens for authority, and a Transparency Log for the record, so delegation is least-authority by construction and every consequential action is attributable and checkable from the record alone. Honest about the bound: containment and attribution, not prevention of a fooled Agent.
- New Terminology entry: Transparency Log.
- Reinforce "Indirect Prompt Injection from Untrusted Content" with a forward reference: model-layer injection cannot be prevented, so pair mitigation with containment and attribution.
- Informative references for the building blocks: DID Core, COSE (RFC 9052), COSE Receipts (RFC 9942), SCITT (RFC 9943), UCAN.
- Add Michael Lavelle to the author list (Orie first, Michael second; docname unchanged).

## Notes

- The added text composes only ratified or widely deployed standards. It does not cite any unpublished work.
- Register kept informational (SHOULD / MAY), matching the rest of the document.
- Drafted with AI assistance.
- This is a Contribution under BCP 78/79. The co-authorship addition is proposed for @OR13 to accept on merge.

Opened as a draft for review and discussion.

comments.body: I don't think we should be citing DIDs in this document, we should focus on things we have found useful in developing software with AI.

I think this is good to comment on, but we should avoid being prescriptive of solutions... I think we should start with voluntary scope management, such as system prompts that know your role, and org chart, and guidance to the agent to not attempt to perform actions their operator won't be able to review. We should avoid talking about securing trajectories, unless we can show its impact on velocity or product dev.

Agreed. Dropped the DID, object-capability, COSE, and SCITT references entirely, along with the Transparency Log term. Nothing in the revision cites or depends on that tech. It now sticks to the scope-management practice we actually use.

Reworked per your steer. The subsection is now "Acting Beyond an Operator's Authority" and leads with voluntary scope management through context engineering: giving the Agent its operator's role and the org chart as durable Context so it declines actions its operator could not get reviewed, and asks for the approval or expert review the work warrants. Removed the prescriptive enforcement framing and anything about securing trajectories, and kept it to keeping the Agent in bounds cheaply, in the prompt, without slowing delivery.

pulls.title: Add a Context Flows section with two diagrams
pulls.author: OR13
pulls.body:
Why: the draft defines the Shared Message Bus, the Issue Tracker, Management Sessions, Trajectories and Evals separately, but never shows how they relate. Two aasvg figures, in a new `# Context Flows` section placed after "Agents on the Shared Message Bus".

## Figure 1 — team coordination (§6)

Humans and a standalone Agent on the shared venues; the Shared Message Bus and Issue Tracker side by side; a Management Session between those venues and the work; worker Agent Sessions below it writing progress back into the tracker.

The prose reads the figure in four moves: shared venues (an Agent may post on a human's behalf or under its own identity); broadcast vs. directed distribution, which is why both venues exist; the Management Session as the natural place to batch Context Farming rather than letting each worker interrupt a human; and worker sessions recording progress so the durable record lives in the org's systems rather than in Agent state.

Worker boxes use the draft's existing term **worker Agent Session** (see the `Agent Harness` and `Management Session` entries in Terminology) rather than introducing a new one.

## Figure 2 — `single agent evals` (§6.1)

Titled exactly `single agent evals`. Narrows to one session: Task → Agent Session (holding the Agent Reasoning ⇄ Agent Tools loop) → two paths out, left to Trajectory → Eval, right to MCP client → MCP server.

**MCP placement.** MCP hangs off Agent Tools, not off the Agent. The consequence drawn in the prose: two Agents on the same LLM in the same Harness, differing only in which MCP servers they are pointed at, are for practical purposes different Agents — so an Eval that does not record the available tools is incomplete.

**Session identifier.** One example UUID `aca20594-89e9-4a0b-b1a3-28e80e3e5540` appears twice, on the Agent Session and again on the Trajectory, so the join is visible in the figure rather than only asserted. Added a `Session Identifier` Terminology entry.

**The three MCP tools — the one thing worth arguing about.** `read_text_file`, `browser_snapshot` and `search_code` are each verified against the server that exposes them (note it is `read_text_file`, not `read_file` — the filesystem server renamed it). But "most frequently used" is **not directly measurable**: no public per-tool call-frequency telemetry exists, and directory installs, views and search volume are proxies for popularity rather than counts of use. The text says so explicitly and notes this ranking should age faster than the rest of the document. The more durable point offered alongside it: all three read from a source the Agent did not author, which is the class of tool through which indirect prompt injection arrives.

## Supporting changes

- New Terminology entries: `Model Context Protocol (MCP)` (MCP was not named anywhere in the draft before this) and `Session Identifier`.
- New informative references: `MCP`, `MCP-SERVERS`, `MCP-PLAYWRIGHT`, `MCP-GITHUB`, `MCP-DIRECTORY`.
- New anchors so the figures can cross-reference existing text: `{#terminology}`, `{#indirect-prompt-injection}`, `{#supply-chain}`, `{#credential-leakage}`.

## Verification

- ASCII fallbacks are 68 and 69 columns (limit 72); `xml2rfc` reports no warnings on `--text` or `--html`.
- All cross-references resolve; captions render as `Figure 1: …` and `Figure 2: single agent evals`.

## Note for anyone building locally

Requires **aasvg 0.4.3**. 0.5.x emits a `<style>` element with `light-dark()` CSS that the RFC 7996 SVG profile rejects (`Did not expect element style there`). Also: `kramdown-rfc` memoizes aasvg output in `.refcache/kdrfc-*-svg_tool_process-*.cache`, so figure edits appear to do nothing until that cache is cleared.

Separately, `lib/.venv` in the checkout points at a moved Python 3.13, so `make` fails; built with `kramdown-rfc | xml2rfc` directly. Unrelated to this change.
